result.headline: The +100 board-full bonus moved the GA's test mean by only about +1.8 apples (47.9 vs 46.2 across 5 seeds), well inside the baseline's ±2.7 seed spread, so the best bonus run (52.5) looking better than the worst baseline run (43.7) is luck, not skill.
result.summary:
The GA (genetic algorithm: evolving a population of networks by selection and mutation) scored 44.2 on this run's test games (100 fixed-seed games, 95% ended by hitting its own body, 28 steps per apple). Across the five baseline seeds it averaged 46.15 with a spread of ±2.71 (range 43.68–50.15). Its learning curve climbed from about 0 to 31 by minute 1.7, then flattened at about 44 from minute 4.6 onward while population_mean kept rising slowly to 36.5. Training and test agree (44.29 vs 44.2), so the GA's score is trustworthy.

The DQN (Deep Q-learning: a network that predicts the value of each move from remembered experience) scored 20.82 on test (79% body crashes, 21% wall crashes, 8 steps per apple). Its five-seed mean was 20.94 ± 0.8. Its training mean (15.3) is lower than its test score because training moves include random exploration. Its curve rose quickly and then stayed roughly flat between 14 and 17 from minute 1 onward. The bonus runs gave the DQN the same mean (20.94), as expected since it almost never filled the board.

The bonus group's GA five-seed mean was 47.93 (range 41.85–52.52), +1.8 over baseline. Paired by seed, the differences run from −2.4 to +5.2, and with 5 seeds a t-test gives about t≈1.4, which is not distinguishable from zero. The bonus fired in only 2 of 500 bonus test games (one win each on seeds 102 and 103), and no baseline test game was won. Training did reach 97 apples (a full board) in the baseline too, so full boards happen, just rarely.
result.diagnosis:
The +100 win bonus is rarely triggered, because filling all 97 free squares on a 10×10 board almost never happens in a test game. Its effect on the GA is therefore on the order of a couple of rare games per 500, which is far below what a single seed can resolve. The observed +1.8 mean difference is the kind of gap you get by chance when each seed's GA ends at a different point of a noisy evolution; the GA's own spread (±2.7) is larger than the effect. The DQN is unaffected for the same reason, and its tiny spread (±0.8) shows it is much more stable than the evolved GA.

The GA is also noisier because its fitness is measured on only 3 games per network, and each generation's winners depend on which seed's random games they happened to get. The DQN ended in body crashes, which suggests a short planning horizon (gamma 0.95 values rewards only about 20 moves ahead) in a game where avoiding one's own tail needs longer foresight. The GA reached about 165 million environment steps in 10 minutes against the DQN's 1.3 million, because the GA's per-step cost is far lower (about 260k steps per second against about 2.5k).
result.learned: A single run is one sample. Before you credit a change, compare the mean across seeds and check whether the ranges overlap; picking the best run of one group against the worst of another always makes a useless change look useful.
result.prediction_check: Held: the bonus did not change results beyond the seed spread, though one bonus run (52.5) did beat the worst baseline run (43.7) as predicted, which is the trap the lesson warns about.

recommendations.title: Score each GA network on 10 games
recommendations.why: The GA's fitness uses only 3 games per network, so a lucky game can make a weak network look strong; if fitness noise is part of the spread, more games should shrink it. This tests whether luck in training, not only in testing, limits the GA.
recommendations.change: Raise the GA's games per network from 3 to 10.
recommendations.prediction: GA test mean stays within the baseline seed range (43–50) but its seed spread narrows; a clear gain above 50 would show fitness noise was costing skill.
recommendations.question: Does less noisy fitness raise the GA's skill in the same 10 minutes, or does it just slow generations?

recommendations.title: Let the DQN plan further ahead
recommendations.why: The DQN ends almost every test game by crashing into its own body (79%), which suggests it can't see far enough ahead to avoid trapping itself. Raising gamma from 0.95 to 0.99 makes it value rewards further in the future.
recommendations.change: Raise the DQN's gamma from 0.95 to 0.99.
recommendations.prediction: DQN test mean rises from 20.8 toward 24–28 apples, with the body-crash share staying high or falling only slightly.
recommendations.question: Is the DQN's ceiling caused by a short planning horizon?

recommendations.title: Test a bigger GA population
recommendations.why: The GA's curve flattened at about 44 from minute 4.6, so the question is whether the search is short of variety (too few networks per generation) or of time. A population of 1000 trades generations for variety at the same wall-clock time.
recommendations.change: Raise the GA population from 200 to 1000.
recommendations.prediction: GA test mean lands between 40 and 48, with no clear gain; a result above 50 would be a real improvement beyond the baseline seed range.
recommendations.question: Is the GA limited by the number of generations or by the diversity within each generation?

ideas.title: Paired seed comparison with an interval
ideas.what: When two seed groups are compared, show the per-seed paired differences, their mean, and a rough 95% interval, with a plain note when the interval includes zero.
ideas.why: The bonus group looked better than baseline in its best run, but its paired mean difference (+1.8, paired t≈1.4 over 5 seeds) is consistent with zero, and the dashboard shows only the ranges.
ideas.expected: Learners would reach the correct 'no real difference' conclusion without hand-computing statistics; the bonus comparison would show a 95% interval of roughly −1 to +5 apples.

ideas.title: Count how often each reward fires
ideas.what: In the test summary, report how many test games triggered each reward feature (win, starve, death) alongside the ended counts.
ideas.why: The win bonus fired in only 2 of 500 bonus test games, and the learner had to infer its rarity from the ended table; a direct count would show at once whether a reward can matter.
ideas.expected: A learner could tell in seconds that a reward with a count of 2 cannot explain a difference of several apples.
